title: York cop Remo Romano found guilty of dangerous driving in 3rd trial
subtitle: Det.-Const. Remo Romano found guilty in fatal collision that claimed life of Carla Abogado
article: After three criminal trials, York Regional Police Det.-Const. Remo Romano has been found guilty of one count of dangerous driving causing death.
The verdict came down Jan. 24 at Toronto's University court after a jury deliberated for less than 24 hours.
It's in relation to a fatal crash that Romano was involved in while on stake-out duty.
While trying to catch up with the rest of his unit, Romano began speeding, driving at least 109 km/h in a 60 km/h zone on St. Clair Avenue East in February 2014.
His Ford F-150 struck and killed Carla Abogado, 18, of Toronto, who was exiting a bus and crossing the street on her way home.
During the first trial in May 2016, the jury was unable to reach a verdict. Months later, in September, Romano was acquitted.
During those first two trials, Abogado's behaviour, namely, the fact that she was jaywalking and possibly listening to music, was a significant factor.
However, the Crown appealed the acquittal because of the judge's comments regarding Abogado's behaviour. In the third trial, only Romano's driving was considered.
"Most significantly, the trial judge made irrelevant and adverse comments about Ms. Abogado's conduct," Justice David Paciocco said in his decision.
During the first trial, the Crown argued police were chasing a suspect vehicle, but had no idea who was in the white van and no arrest was imminent.
An expert for the Crown further suggested had Romano been driving 80 km/h, he might have been able to see Abogado or swerve.
The defence, meanwhile, told the court police officers are exempt from the Highway Traffic Act while in "execution of duty".
Despite Romano writing in his notes that he was approaching "a slope in an area of darkness", he said he was justified in his speed while on duty at 8:12 p.m.
"My hands, as funny as it sounds, were at 10 and 2, (I was) looking at the road," he said.
Through tears, he described the moment he hit Abogado.
"No I did not (see her)," the father-of-three from Woodbridge told the court. "I was trying to get in on the play and help the team."
Abogado's father, a staple during the four years of court appearances, said the family is unsure how to feel following the decision.
"Right now, it's a mixed feeling," said Guillermo Abogado. "We're feeling relieved because it's finally over, but at the same time, our daughter won't be coming back."

Todd Sepkowski, president of the York Regional Police Association, said he is unsure if the public realizes what these types of decisions do to policing, suggesting he might be giving new advice to officers going forward.
"I can't expect anyone to speed, put in this position," he said, referring to an officer wanting to break the speed limit to do their job.
Although Romano's future is unclear, the bar deciding whether an officer is fired or can remain with the force has traditionally been whether or not he or she serves a custodial sentence.
This might be changed in the near future, when changes to the Police Services Act are ushered in, so that services might be able to terminate officers "with cause".
Dangerous driving causing death often results in a jail sentence, however, it is not to exceed 14 years, according to Canadian law.

"This was a terrible tragedy that has had a devastating effect on all those involved," said Const. Laura Nicolle. "Detective Constable Romano has been on administrative duties since the charges were laid and that will continue until the outcome of all criminal proceedings regarding this matter have concluded."
Romano will be sentenced March 14.
